newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Govt snuggles up to Colston.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Govt snuggles up to Colston.

text.p: The Australian government is reacting amicably to Independent senator Mal Colston's concerns over the Telstra privatisation.
Since Colston, a Labor defector, is one of the two Independent senators whose support the government needs for the privatisation bill, the warm response is not surprising.
But it is important to note that it is happening; and it is worth taking note of the words that the government is using.

Asked on Tuesday to detail his concerns, Colston said: "One of them is the decentralised nature of Queensland and the way that Telstra employees are actually working in areas outside of the metropolitan areas.
"My concern is that those Telecom employees remain where they are, and I'm talking especially of operators. One can have operators anywhere, I suppose..."
Asked if he would seek guarantees for Queensland, he added: "If I decided to support the Telstra legislation, most definitely yes."
This is one of his concerns, he says, so he must have others that he is not specifying publicly.
Treasurer Peter Costello responded on Wednesday: "If senator Colston has a legitimate point we'll certainly address it, within the framework of making sure it's overall responsible.
"If he wants to say to the government that 'I'm worried about these particular principles' and if we can accommodate them within the context of a responsible project, we are quite happy to talk."
Colston's demand for employment guarantees is absolutely contrary to the reform principles that drive such government policies as this privatisation.

But note that, principles aside, not much might be at stake. As Colston says, one can have "operators" anywhere. It would be surprising if it cost any more to put the directory assistance people in Roma. (It might even be cheaper.)
And just for the record, Colston advanced his stand on Telstra earlier on Wednesday.
Previously he had said that the government might or might not have a mandate for the partial privatisation.
"In some ways (I am) favourably disposed, but there are a few things that I'd like to talk to the government about," he said on television on Wednesday.
